title: Romeo and Juliet: Why, Not Where
description: A balcony the play never names, a bootleg soliloquy, and a thatch fire—Go Deep into why, not where.

questions.question: Stage tradition stuck Juliet on a balcony—but the word "balcony" never appears in the play. Who wrote Romeo and Juliet, where "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" means "why," not "where"?
questions.explanation: Juliet isn't looking for him; she's lamenting that he's a Montague. The balcony is pure stage tradition—props and romance the text never asks for.

questions.question: Shakespeare was baptized April 26, 1564, in which English market town—tradition claims he died on that same calendar date in 1616?
questions.explanation: Only the baptism is on record; April 23 as birthday is neat folklore. He left for London, made a fortune, and came home a gentleman with a coat of arms.

questions.question: After leaving Stratford-upon-Avon for London, he wrote Hamlet—what line opens its famous soliloquy?
questions.answer: To be or not to be
acceptedAnswers: To be or not to be
to be or not to be
to be, or not to be
choices: Now is the winter of our discontent
questions.explanation: In the 1603 "bad quarto," it reads "To be, or not to be—ay, there's the point." The version everyone quotes arrived with the Second Quarto a year later—likely a pirated, half-remembered bootleg vs. the real thing.

questions.question: Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' likely premiered at which Bankside playhouse, built by Shakespeare's company in 1599 from the timbers of their old venue?
questions.explanation: They dismantled the Theatre over Christmas 1598 and carted the timbers across the Thames. In 1613 a stage cannon set the thatch roof alight during Henry VIII; nobody died, but the Globe burned.

questions.question: Beyond the Globe stage, he wrote poetry too—how many sonnets appear in his 1609 collection dedicated to the mysterious "Mr. W.H."?
questions.explanation: Publisher Thomas Thorpe's dedication still baffles scholars. Sonnet 145 may pun on his wife, Anne Hathaway: "'I hate' from hate away she threw"—hate-away, Hathaway.

imageHint: A historic 1623 folio that preserved many of his plays for posterity

easterEgg.title: Ay, there's the point
easterEgg.text: The 1603 "bad quarto" of Hamlet gives the speech as "To be, or not to be, ay there's the point"—likely a pirated, half-remembered bootleg. The version we know arrives in the 1604 "good quarto."
